title: Dek Agira
author: Laker Grace
desc: Pigeon peas or beans mashed until smooth and creamy and served with shea butter over millet bread — the dish used to anoint traditional leaders in the clans of Lango.
longDesc: Dek agira is mashed pigeon peas with shea butter, and its significance is larger than its method: it is used to anoint traditional leaders in the clans of the Lango community, and it is served at traditional weddings. The cooking is a single line in every source — the peas or beans are mashed until smooth and creamy. That is honest and it is all there is. The shea butter, moo yaa, and the kwon kal it is eaten with are what make it a plate rather than a paste.
ingredients: Millet flour, for the accompanying kwon kal
equipment: Masher, or an ogwec stirring stick
steps: Boil the pigeon peas or beans until soft.
Mash them until smooth and creamy.
Serve with shea butter and kwon kal (UGA091).
For the wedding version, peanut butter goes in as well.
chefTips: Smooth and creamy is the whole instruction, and it is all any source gives. Nothing here is invented to pad it out.
Shea butter is not a garnish. Moo yaa is the northern cooking fat and it is what distinguishes dek agira from every mashed-legume dish further south.
Kwon kal — the millet bread in UGA091 — is what it is eaten with, and the pairing is fixed rather than optional.
Peanut butter appears specifically in the wedding preparation, which suggests the plain version is the everyday one.
Dek ngor, UGA092, is the closely related Acholi dish and its fuller method — soak, sun-dry, grind, winnow, boil, mash with an ogwec — is the best available guide to how this one is actually made.
No quantities exist anywhere. The article that covers it is thin on method and rich on ceremony, and that imbalance is itself information about how the dish is transmitted.
It is used to anoint traditional leaders in the Lango clans. That is worth knowing before you cook it casually.
commonMistakes: Substituting butter or oil for shea butter.
Adding peanut butter to the everyday version.
sources: Adapted from the Wikipedia article on Dek Agira, which gives the method as mashing pigeon peas or beans until smooth and creamy and nothing further, lists pigeon peas or beans, shea butter oil, millet flour for the accompanying kwon kal and peanut butter for the wedding preparation, and states explicitly that no quantities are given.

Its cultural content is the article's real substance: the dish is used to anoint traditional leaders in the clans of the Lango community, and it is served at traditional weddings. That is carried here.

Its citations include Daily Monitor 2020 under the headline 'A food to annoint Lango's leaders', Uganda Broadcasting Corporation 2023, and a Slow Food Foundation entry for Alanga Col Black Bean. One of its five citations is a travel listicle, which is noted rather than relied on.
The fuller pigeon-pea processing method in UGA092 is the best available guide to the preparation and is cross-referenced rather than transplanted into the steps here.
reheating: Warm gently with a little water.
healthBenefits: Pigeon peas are high in protein, fibre, folate and potassium.
Shea butter supplies fat-soluble vitamins and is used in small amounts.
Eaten with millet bread it makes a complete protein.
culturalNote: Anointing a clan leader with a food is as strong a statement as a cuisine makes, and the fact that the written record carries the ceremony in detail and the cooking in one sentence tells you the method was never the part that needed writing down. That is true of a great deal of Ugandan food.
